title: Ibrance (palbociclib): US Regulatory Status, Indications, Dosing, and Label Safety Information
summary: Ibrance (palbociclib) is an oral CDK4/6 inhibitor originally approved by the FDA in 2015 and marketed by Pfizer. Its current FDA-approved indications have expanded over time and, as of mid-2026, include use in combination with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant for HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced/metastatic breast cancer, in combination with inavolisib and fulvestrant for a PIK3CA-mutated subset of that same population, and (per a June 2026 FDA approval) in combination with trastuzumab (with or without pertuzumab) and endocrine therapy for maintenance treatment of HR-positive/HER2-positive advanced/metastatic breast cancer. The label does not carry a boxed warning; instead it carries standard Warnings and Precautions for neutropenia, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity, plus required hematologic monitoring. The label states there are no contraindications. Dosing is a standard 125 mg once-daily, 21-days-on/7-days-off cycle, with capsule and tablet formulations differing in food requirements and available dose-reduction steps for hepatic/renal impairment and drug interactions.

claims.text: Ibrance capsules and tablets are both formulated as palbociclib, an oral kinase inhibitor with initial U.S. FDA approval in 2015; the tablet formulation may be taken with or without food, while the capsule formulation must be taken with food.

claims.text: IBRANCE is not an inhibitor of several CYP enzymes, but coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., itraconazole) increases palbociclib exposure, while strong CYP3A inducers (e.g., rifampin) markedly decrease palbociclib exposure; the dose of sensitive CYP3A substrates with narrow therapeutic indices may need to be reduced when co-administered with IBRANCE.

claims.text: Based on findings from animal studies and its mechanism of action, IBRANCE can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman; embryo-fetal toxicity was seen in pregnant rats and rabbits at maternal exposures ≥4 times human clinical exposure (AUC). Females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose, and breastfeeding should be avoided due to lack of data on presence in human milk.

citations.title: full prescribing information for IBRANCE
citations.supporting_text: Based on findings from animal studies and its mechanism of action, IBRANCE can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. In animal reproduction studies, administration of palbociclib to pregnant rats and rabbits during organogenesis resulted in embryo-fetal toxicity at maternal exposures that were ≥4 times the human clinical exposure based on area under the curve (AUC). Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment with IBRANCE and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose. There is no information regarding the presence of palbociclib in human milk, its effects on milk production, or the breastfed infant.

claims.text: Palbociclib is a highly selective small-molecule inhibitor of CDK4 and CDK6 that causes loss of RB1 phosphorylation and induces cell cycle arrest at the G1-S phase in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer cells, with preclinical and phase 2 (PALOMA-1) data showing prolonged progression-free survival when combined with letrozole compared with letrozole alone in postmenopausal, newly diagnosed metastatic HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer.

citations.supporting_text: Palbociclib (Ibrance, Pfizer) is a highly selective small-molecule inhibitor of CDK4 and CDK6, which can be administered orally. It results in loss of RB1 phosphorylation in vitro and leads to cell cycle arrest at the G1-S phase in ER+ breast cancer. ... An open-label randomized phase 2 study involving postmenopausal patients with newly diagnosed metastatic ER+ and human epidermal growth factor receptor (Her-2/neu) negative breast cancer (PALOMA1), showed that palbociclib in combination with letrozole was associated with significantly prolonged PFS when compared with letrozole alone.

claims.text: In the pivotal INAVO120 triplet-combination safety population (n=324), serious adverse reactions occurred in 24% of patients receiving IBRANCE plus inavolisib and fulvestrant, most commonly anemia (1.9%), diarrhea (1.2%), and urinary tract infection (1.2%); common adverse reactions (≥10%) for this combination in the FDA label included neutropenia, leukopenia, decreased lymphocytes, stomatitis, diarrhea, decreased calcium, fatigue, decreased potassium, increased creatinine, increased ALT, nausea, decreased sodium, decreased magnesium, rash, decreased appetite, COVID-19 infection, and headache.

warnings: Some sources (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov protocol appendices, Medscape, Healio, RxList) reflect FDA label information from various past dates and may not capture the most recent label revisions (e.g., 2025-2026 updates including the June 2026 trastuzumab/pertuzumab maintenance approval); where possible, more recent FDA/DailyMed sources were prioritized, but full verbatim confirmation of the very latest complete label was not achieved.

The IBRANCE label explicitly cautions that adverse reaction rates across different trials/combinations cannot be directly compared because trials are conducted under widely varying conditions; cross-regimen comparisons in this section (e.g., aromatase inhibitor vs. fulvestrant vs. inavolisib triplet vs. trastuzumab-based maintenance) should be interpreted with this caveat.

The letrozole-based indication remains under accelerated approval status per the label language retrieved; this regulatory status should be verified against the most current label for any change to full approval.
